newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to stage war games on eve of HK handover.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to stage war games on eve of HK handover.

text.p: Taiwan made final preparations on Sunday for two days of military exercises, ignoring U.S. concerns that such manoeuvres could rile China just one week before it resumes control of Hong Kong.

State television signalled that the Nationalist government hoped to exploit the global attention attracted by the drills, saying Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui planned an important policy statement on Tuesday, the day the war games are scheduled to end.

Lee plans to inspect the games in southern Tainan province and the Taiwan strait, echoing a practice of mainland Chinese leader Jiang Zemin. Jiang regularly reviewed drills and missile tests mounted over eight months in 1995-96 in a clear demonstration of Beijing's resolve to take back Taiwan.
Local media speculated that Lee's statement would relate to ties with the mainland, whose communist forces drove the Nationalists into exile on Taiwan to end a civil war in 1949.

Although they were announced a year ago, the annual live-fire exercises have fuelled controversy because they will be held a week before Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on Jume 30 after 156 years as a British colony.
Concern grew in early June with unconfirmed reports that China could respond with major "counterbalancing" manoeuvres.
The United States added its weight o n June 11, warning both sides against staging exercises during the sensitive run-up to Hong Kong's handover.

"It's best to stand down in times like this and to continue activities that promote goodwill and understanding peace and not to engage in activities that are counter-productive," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington.
Taiwan flatly rejected the U.S. advice, saying the military exercises had nothing to do with the handover.
"They are annual routine exercises, which absolutely are not held to target the Hong Kong handover, and do not harbour any provocative intentions," a defence ministry spokesman said.

He noted that the "Chinese Glory" drills had been a Taiwan tradition since 1984, though in 1995 and 1996 they were scuttled to avoid exacerbating acute military tensions arising from Beijing's exercises in the Taiwan Strait.

Taiwan, still ruled by the Nationalists who were routed by communist mainland forces, espouses reunification -- but not until Beijing embraces a pluralist democracy that ends the communists' constitutional monopoly on power.
Beijing views Taiwan as a rebel-held province and says it will attack the island if it seeks independence.

Monday's military exercises by Taiwan's armed forces, named Chinese Glory No. 13, will showcase not only the high-tech Patriot missiles, but a host of other advanced weapons that Taipei has managed to procure despite Beijing's drive to halt international arms sales to Taiwan.
These include U.S. F-16 and French Mirage fighters, radar-evading "stealth" frigates from France, an array of imported and locally made missiles, and Taiwan's own Indigenous Defence Fighter.
Analysts say the timing is no coincidence.

By staging drills close to Hong Kong's handover, Taiwan is putting teeth behind its oft-stated rejection of the "one country, two systems" model of local autonomy that Beijing is pioneering in Hong Kong and advocates for retaking Taiwan.
"Taiwan wants to make clear that Taiwan is not Hong Kong," military expert Andrew Yang told Reuters.
Live-fire exercises involving the army, air force and the navy start on Tuesday, and Lee and other leaders will be on hand to view the action, officials said.
